Deep learning techniques have gained significant attention for brain tumor segmentation, but classification remains an underutilized approach despite its potential for tailoring treatment strategies to individual patients. This study presents a novel 3D UNet architecture that incorporates contextual information through a convolutional encoder, enabling it to generate relevant spatial features for a fully connected dense layer. This paper presents a novel approach to visual object recognition in complex document images by combining a pre-trained, lightweight ConvNets model with a custom classification layer that can be tailored to specific image content types. The proposed method leverages the robustness of pre-trained ConvNets to learn generic features and relies on dictionary-based representation to identify semantically meaningful objects. By integrating pre-trained ConvNets with dictionary-based representation using a fully connected layer, the approach achieves high accuracy in visual object recognition for datasets with sufficient training data. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective in real-world applications, including dataset-specific recognition, such as in handwritten and machine-printed text recognition, and generic object recognition across various image content types. The approach is further validated through benchmarking on large-scale datasets and real-world applications, resulting in state-of-the-art performance. The implementation details are made publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, the approach is shown to be highly adaptable and can be easily extended to recognize visual objects in real-world images and applications, such as in handwritten and machine-printed text recognition, and in generic object recognition. Significant advancements in neural abstractive summarization have been made, 
yet concerns have arisen about the accuracy of these models, particularly their 
tendency to generate summaries that are overly flattering. Research suggests that 
these models primarily aim to create coherent summaries rather than accurately 
representing the original content. To rectify this issue, we developed a novel 
training framework that guides summarization models to prioritize factual 
accuracy. Our approach involves integrating a reward function that assesses the 
similarity between generated summaries and their original references using 
contextual semantic embeddings. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of 
this method, showcasing improved accuracy, particularly in situations where 
summaries deviate from their original context. Our model also exhibits superior 
fidelity in generating summaries compared to state-of-the-art alternatives. 
Moreover, we demonstrate that our model is resistant to adversarial manipulation, 
as it prioritizes truthfulness above reward signals. Our research has been made 
available on GitHub at https://github.com/Namita-Mudhol/TCA. To facilitate further 
research, we have compiled a dataset of factually inaccurate summaries 
(DebiasedSumm) and a corresponding fact-checking dataset (FactCheckSumm). The 
datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/Namita-Mudhol/DebiasedSumm. In 
addition, we provide code and models for the DebiasedSumm dataset at 
https://github.com/Namita-Mudhol/DebiasedSumm. Our research has been evaluated by 
human evaluators, who have verified the accuracy of our generated summaries. 
Ultimately, we believe that our work marks an important step towards developing 
factually accurate summarization models.

Notably, the derived nonconserved solution to the Fokker-Planck equation is distinct from the previously known conserved solutions. This distinction is attributed to the non-Hermiticity of the harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of WikiGUM in recognizing relationships that other systems often fail to identify, thereby paving the way for improved performance on complex tasks such as question answering and text generation. To simplify this process, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a hybrid recommendation system, incorporating various ranking factors to suggest potential pairs of publications for reference. In the realm of cognitive science, certain characteristics are well-established as having a direct impact on future performance, such as the ability to process multiple tasks simultaneously, spatial reasoning skills, and working memory capacity. Although these traits have been found to be highly effective predictors of future task performance, they are often limited to specific domains. For instance, spatial reasoning skills are particularly valuable in fields like mathematics and geology, whereas working memory capacity is more broadly applicable. This raises an intriguing question: can we identify a set of characteristics that hold the potential to enhance performance in a wide range of tasks, regardless of domain? This paper presents a novel approach to answering this question by leveraging an unsupervised representation learning framework to identify varied task characteristics that can forecast task performance. Our empirical findings demonstrate that these learned characteristics can forecast task performance across different domains. We validate our approach using a dataset of 3,500 tasks across 9 diverse domains and 1,221 human subjects. Our results indicate that these learned characteristics can forecast task performance significantly better than established performance metrics, such as time-to-infinity and RTA10. Moreover, our approach has been shown to be highly effective in forecasting task performance in a new, unseen dataset, yielding a substantial improvement over the baseline performance. This suggests that these learned characteristics possess broad domain adaptability and can potentially be applied to a wide range of tasks across different domains. Our findings have significant implications for the development of a general-purpose cognitive framework that can forecast task performance in any given scenario. Our approach has been made publicly available on GitHub. We encourage researchers to explore the potential of these learned characteristics in forecasting task performance across different domains. Cache side-channel attacks have been a significant threat to software security for years, and recent high-profile breaches involving the L1 cache have highlighted the need for more effective ways to detect and prevent cache-based vulnerabilities. However, current spike-based training algorithms have limitations in their accuracy and speed of convergence, often relying on gradient estimation through integration over time.  In contrast, we present a novel approach called Spikemax, which employs a more direct and efficient method for loss estimation.  By using a maximum operator to approximate the loss, Spikemax can be trained with a single time step, eliminating the need for integration and significantly accelerating its convergence speed.  Furthermore, Spikemax can be combined with existing gradient-based training methods to achieve superior results, demonstrating its potential in real-world applications.  Our experiments show that Spikemax can achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art gradient-based methods on MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, while achieving a significant reduction in training time.  By integrating Spikemax into a neural network, we observed a substantial improvement in accuracy, with an enhancement of 2.1% and 1.3% on MNIST and CIFAR10 respectively, when compared to a baseline model.  Our results demonstrate that Spikemax can be a valuable addition to existing spike-based training techniques and has the potential to accelerate the development of efficient and accurate spiking neural networks. Researchers have attempted to address this issue by developing methods that pinpoint the most crucial intervals based on specific goals. In the context of human-agent team collaboration, the dynamic team structure and subsequent state of perception are crucial factors. However, the current research methods in understanding human agents' team preferences often rely on either a single, static team structure or simplified preferences. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel dataset created by analyzing the team preferences of 1,500 players through the game Overcooked 2, a platform that allows for diverse team preferences. Our dataset expands on previous research by incorporating multiple team structures, diverse team preferences, and detailed measures of players' perceptions. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive set of indicators for team preferences and perception, encompassing variables such as spatial awareness, attention, and workload, which can be utilized to enhance the validity of human agents' team preferences in future research. Our research demonstrates that our proposed indicators effectively capture players' team preferences and outperform previously established measures. The dataset and indicators are now available for public access. Our findings have the potential to inform the development of human-agent team dynamics and improve the design of human agents that can effectively collaborate with humans. The ultimate goal is to enable the creation of human agents that can seamlessly integrate into various real-world collaborative settings. The research also aims to establish a foundation for understanding human agents' team preferences and perception. By making our data and indicators publicly available, we can accelerate the advancement of human-agent team dynamics research. We introduce a new mixed-integer linear programming model, circular and bipartite vertex cover (C&BVC), to find a perfect vertex cover in bipartite graphs. Our model outperforms existing disjunctive vertex cover approaches and develops into a fast and effective heuristic. Experimental results demonstrate that the C&BVC model combined with our developed heuristic delivers superior time performance compared to current methods, specifically CPLEX and disjunctive vertex cover models, across multiple real-world benchmark instances. Our innovative approach can be easily adapted for finding minimum weight perfect vertex covers and facilitates efficient weighted vertex cover calculations. Furthermore, we establish a proof that the C&BVC model is weakly NP-hard, while acknowledging that disjunctive vertex cover models are strongly NP-hard. Our research paves the way for further investigation of the C&BVC model and its related weighted vertex cover problems. This study delves into the structural properties of the bidirectional market network and leverages transfer entropy to investigate its function. The bidirectional market network combines elements of social networks and financial transactions, creating a unique network environment. Analyzing this network enables the examination of a vast array of actors and transactions, providing valuable insights into the interconnected dynamics. The research findings indicate that the bidirectional market network exhibits a scale-free distribution, characteristic of its static structure. Furthermore, this network demonstrates a unique pattern of dynamic interactions, with evidence of multiplexity and a modular structure in its temporal dynamics. The results of transfer entropy analysis reveal a complex pattern of information flow between actors within the network. The distribution of this information flow is found to be uniform, with certain actors exhibiting a greater capacity to receive information. The research demonstrates that the bidirectional market network exhibits distinct characteristics in its static and dynamic configurations, with implications for our understanding of information flow and decision-making processes in financial transactions. The study's findings also highlight the potential for further investigation into the complex dynamics of this network. Ultimately, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between social and financial interactions within the bidirectional market network. The research also underscores the need for continued analysis of this network's complex properties and dynamics. The accompanying software, Labelr, enables the implementation of these findings and facilitates the replication of the study's methods. This research focuses on causal order and its impact on gravitational thermodynamics in specific spacetime configurations. We examine how causal order influences the thermodynamic properties of causal diamonds and causal crystals in both flat and AdS backgrounds. Building on the principles of gravitational thermodynamics, our findings demonstrate that causal order does not affect Bekenstein-Hawking area laws or the ground state entropy of causal crystals, implying it's an irrelevant factor at a local level. However, we discover that causal order plays a significant role at the boundary, where it alters the entropy of causal diamonds and thus the grand potential of causal crystals. Consequently, the pressure of causal crystals is influenced by their size and shape, as well as the surrounding spacetime environment. Our findings also show that causal order affects the speed of sound in causal crystals. We further explore the thermodynamic properties of causal crystals in AdS spacetimes and discuss the implications of our research. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of causal thermodynamics and the possibility of measuring the speed of sound in causal crystals using current technology. Lastly, we outline the future directions for this research.

In speaker authentication, standardized Mel-frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCC) features are typically computed using fixed, non-adaptive parameters. This paper presents a new method where the speaker estimation and acoustic modeling components within a speaker verification or identification system learn MFCC features jointly through a self-supervised process. This is achieved by incorporating a speaker estimation model that directly calculates d-vector embeddings, which are subsequently used to train an MFCC extractor. This process involves training an MFCC extractor to transform short-time windowed audio into d-vector embeddings, which are computed using a speaker estimation model. This allows the entire system to be trained end-to-end without relying on traditional cepstral extraction algorithms. This approach is referred to as trainable MFCCs (T-MFCCs). Experiments conducted on the VoxCeleb dataset for speaker verification and on the VoxCeleb and SITW datasets for speaker identification demonstrate that T-MFCCs achieve comparable performance to baseline algorithms using Sinc-based MFCCs. Notably, the T-MFCC method also exhibits improved computational efficiency, with a 50% reduction in processing time. This is attributed to the fact that T-MFCCs eliminate the need for the traditional MFCC extraction process. This work is anticipated to contribute to the development of more efficient and scalable speaker systems in the future. Feature toggles are widely utilized in software development to enable the simultaneous deployment of conflicting features, thus enabling the rapid delivery of software. However, their implementation can complicate software architecture, ultimately resulting in bugs. Given the growing importance of continuous delivery, it is crucial to understand the relationship between feature toggles and bugs. Our research aims to investigate the prevalence of feature toggles and their correlation with bugs in open-source projects. Our analysis of 1,014 popular GitHub projects revealed that 55% employ feature toggles, with a notable increase in their usage over the past three years. Our study also found that branch merges are more frequent in projects that use feature toggles, although this correlation may be influenced by other factors. Our investigation into the most commonly used feature toggle patterns and their distribution in the project's code did not yield conclusive results. Our research offers valuable insights for practitioners and researchers to better understand the role of feature toggles in software development. Our findings suggest that further research is needed to establish a clear connection between feature toggles and bugs. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved Vocal Voice Transformation technology. However, existing methods often struggle to achieve high-quality results, particularly when attempting to transform vocal characteristics beyond the realm of natural human capabilities. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel method, DiffSVC, based on a diffusion process. By leveraging a latent diffusion model and a conditional model, DiffSVC can effectively handle complex transformations and produce high-quality outputs. Our approach involves a two-step training process, where the model is first taught to generate speech from a target voice and then to reverse the process, allowing it to synthesize speech with the desired voice's characteristics. To optimize this two-step process, we incorporate a conditional model that enables the model to generate speech that accurately captures the nuances of the target voice. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DiffSVC, particularly in situations where the target voice exhibits extreme characteristics. Furthermore, our method allows for the seamless integration of prior vocal characteristics, enabling the generation of speech with the desired voice's characteristics. Deep learning models have achieved significant success in computer vision tasks, but they often struggle with the "few instance learning" problem, specifically in recognizing intricate objects. This problem is particularly challenging for agile alignment methods like deformable group convolution (FGC) and adaptive multi-scale alignment (AMA), as they rely on a sufficient number of instances to function effectively. To address this limitation, we developed a meta-filter that can identify instances with poor alignment and selectively exclude them from the agile alignment pipeline. This filter is integrated with FGC and AMA to create a robust alignment filter (RAF), which significantly enhances the performance of these methods in the few instance learning setting. Experimental results demonstrate that RAF outperforms traditional agile alignment methods by a substantial margin of 8.8% and 10.4% mAP, respectively. Moreover, our code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository "zengj2019/RAF". The results of our experiments also reveal that the alignment errors in the few instance learning setting are highly correlated and can be effectively addressed by removing the instances with the highest alignment errors. Based on this finding, we developed a novel method called the "alignment error removal" (AER) technique, which involves removing the 20% instances with the highest alignment errors. When applied to FGC and AMA, AER yields substantial performance improvements of 11.1% and 8.4% mAP, respectively. Notably, our approach is the first to tackle the few instance learning problem, and our innovative alignment error removal technique has the potential to enhance the performance of agile alignment methods in various few instance learning scenarios. This work is expected to inspire further research on the few instance learning problem and the technique of alignment error removal. A specific type of ordered framework, known as an indexed matrix framework, consists of a matrix with assigned labels for each element. These labels are essential in determining the framework's properties. In particular, we examine a specific class of frameworks, namely those with a cyclic structure and n-fold symmetry, and investigate how many distinct frameworks with this property exist for a given n. Our research also provides a mathematical formula to calculate the number of such frameworks, and we explore the relationship between this number and certain combinatorial concepts, including partition diagrams and minimal polynomials. Furthermore, we establish a connection between this problem and graph theory, specifically the concept of a graph's automorphism group. However, we are unable to establish a general formula for a generic n-tensor, and we leave this problem as a subject of future research. Our research also includes a list of open problems and areas of future investigation. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop methods that balance data utility with privacy requirements. In this study, we introduce an innovative approach that utilizes a deep neural network-based autoencoder to maintain data utility while making minimal changes to the original dataset. By employing multiple autoencoders for each class, our method effectively preserves data utility within class, thus ensuring that the encoded representations remain meaningful. Moreover, our method has been successfully applied to the ImSitu dataset, which contains real-world personal data. The results show that the utility of the modified data is comparable to that of the original data, thus underscoring the effectiveness of our approach in balancing privacy and utility. This paper introduces three comprehensive benchmark resources for evaluating word embedding models in the Tatar language: Resemblance, Association, and Analogies. The proposed benchmarks are derived from English-Tatar parallel corpora and translated from English examples. The datasets are accompanied by a word embedding evaluation toolkit, allowing users to compare the performance of various word embedding models using the provided benchmarks. An experimental analysis of the presented datasets is also included, providing insights into the effectiveness of different word embedding models. The evaluation results reveal that models trained on large datasets, such as the Wikipedia corpus, achieve better results in semantic and syntactic analogies, whereas models trained on smaller datasets, such as the Word2Vec model, perform better in assessing word similarity. The performance of word embedding models in the English language is found to be significantly better than in the Tatar language, with the largest gap observed in the "Analogies" benchmark. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of the Tatar language's limited training data on the performance of word embedding models. The evaluation toolkit and the created benchmark resources are made available to the public under the permissive MIT open source license. In point cloud processing, data reduction is a crucial step that involves selecting a subset of representative points to minimize computational demands. Despite numerous point selection methods available, such as random sampling and Poisson-disc sampling, they often fall short in preserving the overall shape of the data due to their inherent limitations. By representing the data as a hypergraph, we formulate an optimization problem that identifies the most optimal point set for data reduction. Our method, which we call hypergraph point selection, offers several key benefits, including the ability to adapt to changing sampling densities, the preservation of data features, and the elimination of artifacts that can occur with point selection methods. Through extensive testing, we demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing point selection techniques in terms of accuracy and effectiveness. Additionally, we show that it is well-suited for real-time applications that require high levels of resilience and efficiency. This paper introduces the $m$-paralogarithmic synthesis and the $m$-paralogarithmic expansion, along with the $m$-paralogarithmic revival monomials, which enable the creation of legal formal series under specific conditions. These new methods can be seen as an extension of the paralogarithmic synthesis and expansion introduced by Abate and Gentile. We demonstrate that the $m$-paralogarithmic revival monomials can be effectively utilized in the $m$-paralogarithmic synthesis and provide an example of a legal formal series that cannot be derived from any of the previously known synthesis techniques. Furthermore, we establish that the $m$-paralogarithmic revival monomials constitute a canonical basis for the $m$-paralogarithmic expansion. To enhance semi-supervised learning, particularly for vision tasks, we introduce an innovative approach called FlexMatch. FlexMatch consists of two key components: a curriculum learning mechanism and a multi-stage loss function. The curriculum learning component involves a dynamic approach where difficult samples are gradually introduced to the model as it improves, mimicking the process of a human teacher. This approach draws on the concept of self-paced learning. The multi-stage loss component involves a two-step process where initial soft pseudo-labels are generated for all samples, followed by a more stringent hard pseudo-labeling stage for a subset of highly confident examples. The two stages are dynamically adjusted based on the uncertainty of each sample's label. Our experiments demonstrate that FlexMatch outperforms existing methods in semi-supervised image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks, particularly in low-data scenarios. Furthermore, our code has been released on GitHub at: https://github.com/megvii-research/flexmatch. Our findings are supported by a comprehensive ablation study, which reveals the significance of each FlexMatch component in achieving superior results. Notably, the results of our ablation study align with our theoretical expectations. FlexMatch has been successfully applied to real-world scenarios, yielding impressive results when training data is limited. When compared to fully supervised methods, FlexMatch has achieved notable performance gains in object detection and segmentation tasks, particularly when the amount of training data is severely restricted. When paired with a fully supervised model, FlexMatch has achieved a notable boost in performance, resulting in a 2% increase in object detection mAP and 5% increase in segmentation mIoU. FlexMatch has been successfully integrated into MMSeggy, an open-source deep learning framework, and has been made available for public use. Our results have been presented at the 31st IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2021). Notably, our work has been recognized with a Best Paper Award. By incorporating temporal attention mechanisms and a low-rank matrix, the model enhances its ability to forecast future values by identifying relevant patterns in past data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed network in achieving higher accuracy than current state-of-the-art models for both short-term and long-term forecasting of financial time-series data. This framework can be extended to other domains, such as image processing and other applications, where interactions between consecutive data points are relevant. This research explores the conditional independence test for two variables given a third variable in a region. The existing standard permutation test approach has a flaw in that it fails to account for regional heterogeneity. We develop a new permutation test based on permutation tests within each sub-region rather than the entire region. The proposed test exhibits several favorable properties, including robustness to both noise in low-probability areas and highly consistent data in high-probability areas. Additionally, our results demonstrate the test's resilience to both sparse and concentrated forms of dependence. Through simulation studies, our results show that the test performs well in various scenarios, especially when the signal is present in a small portion of the region, and outperforms the standard permutation test in real data applications. The new test is also computationally efficient and can handle large data sets. The theoretical framework of the test is further expanded to accommodate multiple variables and diverse independence models. The proposed method is applied to a real-world example involving solar radiation patterns in Australia. The study reveals that the conditional independence test detects a relationship between solar radiation levels and elevation in southwestern Australia. The findings suggest that the test is effective in identifying regional patterns of dependence that may be masked by traditional permutation tests. This research investigates the performance of a wireless-powered sensor network that utilizes non-orthogonal multiple access techniques for simultaneous data transmission from multiple sensors to their respective base stations. We analyze the average achievable data rate for each sensor group in this network, considering factors such as channel quality and the power harvested from the base station's transmitted signal. We establish a mathematical expression to determine the average data rate for sensors within close proximity to the base station and validate our findings with numerical results, observing that increasing the transmitted power in the base station enhances the average data rate for nearby sensors, but also increases interference for sensors farther away, resulting in a reduced average data rate. Moreover, we note that the average data rate for sensors at optimal distances from the base station is maximized when the transmission power is moderate, while increasing the number of supported sensors in the network also decreases the average data rate due to increased interference. For sensors at suboptimal distances, the optimal transmission power is lower than that required for sensors at optimal distances. Additionally, we find that the average data rate for sensors at suboptimal distances is maximized when the number of supported sensors is minimal. Our research provides valuable insights into the theoretical performance of a wireless-powered sensor network that utilizes non-orthogonal multiple access techniques for simultaneous data transmission from multiple sensors to their respective base stations. The findings of this study can serve as a guide for the development of future wireless-powered sensor networks that utilize non-orthogonal multiple access techniques. Quantum field theory's field operators are structured as combinations of a base state and variations thereof. This structure leads to a representation problem since these operators' correlation functions typically exhibit entangled properties. To resolve this issue, we reframe the field operators as a form of quantum operations that treat a system's space as a single entity. This novel interpretation allows us to analyze quantum field operator properties without imposing separability constraints, thereby illuminating the field operators' representation of quantum systems comprising multiple components. Furthermore, we establish a connection between this interpretation and the standard matrix formulation of quantum systems, thereby demonstrating that the field operators' representation of quantum systems is consistent with established understanding. This research demonstrates that quantum field operators' complex structures encode valuable physical information and offers a fresh perspective on the field operators that may prove beneficial in resolving open problems in quantum field theory. The study's findings also have implications for the interpretation of quantum field operators beyond the realm of quantum field theory. The ability to repair visual information and recover from visual loss is crucial for self-mobility and daily activities. This study explores the visual system's capacity to repair visual defects caused by obstacles or visual impairment in dynamic environments. A comprehensive dataset featuring various visual repair scenarios is presented, accompanied by an assessment of the visual repair capability of healthy and visually impaired individuals. Our findings demonstrate that the visual repair capability of healthy individuals and low-vision individuals differs, with the latter exhibiting reduced repair capability. This discovery highlights the need to consider the visual system's inherent repair capabilities when designing visual prosthetics and assistive technology. Furthermore, our research reveals that incorporating real-world data into training deep learning models enhances their robustness to natural variations. This work has the potential to advance the development of visual prosthetics and assistive systems by leveraging the visual system's inherent repair capabilities. The field of video recognition has garnered significant attention, with a wide range of applications including human action recognition, video retrieval, and surveillance. Recent years have seen the development of several video recognition datasets, which have enabled the creation of new models. However, these models are often limited by their domain specificity and inability to generalize to other domains. To address this challenge, this study proposes a new approach to video recognition that leverages the capabilities of a pre-trained image classifier. By adapting the image classifier to video data, we demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving comparable performance to that of state-of-the-art video recognition models. To this end, we introduce a new framework that utilizes a pre-trained image classifier and a video encoder, which we train on a large-scale video dataset. We evaluate the transferred model on a range of video recognition tasks, including action recognition, video retrieval, and surveillance, and demonstrate its competitive performance in comparison to other existing models. Furthermore, we show that the transferred model can be fine-tuned to specific domains using a limited amount of video data, thereby enabling its adaptation to new domains. In order to address this knowledge gap, scientists have turned to simulations of star formation within turbulent molecular clouds, with the aim of understanding how stars initially form from the gravitational collapse of small, self-gravitating fragments within these clouds.  This process is believed to be the key to explaining the emergence of the first stars and the formation of planetary systems. Arabic speech transcription for non-native speakers, known as Arabizi, is a complex task that requires accurate transcription. Arabizi transcription systems for Tunisia face data scarcity issues due to limited resources. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages multi-task sequence forecasting to generate four distinct tiers of Arabizi transcription. These tiers comprise the original audio, Transliteration, Translation, and Translation Intent. By incorporating multiple tasks, our system enhances performance and increases the effectiveness of transfer learning. Notably, translating intent proves to be the most demanding task. We also introduce a new dataset, comprising 20,000 manually annotated samples, and evaluate the effectiveness of transformer-based sequence-to-sequence models trained on this dataset. We present an innovative method for refining the algebraic multigrid (AMG) operator through reinforcement learning, which iteratively optimizes the transfer matrix and stopping criterion parameters. Our approach diverges from conventional methods by formulating AMG refinement as a sequential decision-making process, guided by a reward function that assesses the multigrid convergence factor. This formulation enables the simultaneous exploration and exploitation of the vast solution space, ultimately yielding a more efficient and robust AMG operator. Our proposed method outperforms existing AMG operators, as evidenced by its superior performance on a range of benchmark problems featuring complex PDEs. Furthermore, the trained multigrid operator demonstrates robustness across diverse materials and mesh sizes, while its adaptability is also extended to solving linear systems directly, eliminating the need for preconditioning. This research marks a significant advancement towards the development of a universal multigrid operator, applicable to a wide variety of problems. The goal of indexing is to efficiently locate specific data in a database, often achieved through pre-defined indexes that are costly to maintain. A promising approach to avoid upfront indexing decisions is offline indexing, where the best strategy is determined at query time. Offline strategies leverage a dataset's statistics to estimate query distributions, allowing for the identification of the most cost-effective strategies. However, determining the optimal approach remains a complex challenge. A recent method uses neural networks to estimate costs and found them effective in identifying top-performing strategies. This study investigates whether neural networks can be used as a standalone component in offline indexing strategies. We propose a novel approach that integrates neural networks with existing statistical data, demonstrating its potential to outperform the state-of-the-art. Our experiments on real-world datasets show that this approach can identify the best strategies, with a notable improvement in identifying the best strategy for sequential workloads. Notably, this work is the first to demonstrate that neural networks can be used as a standalone component in offline indexing strategies. Our findings suggest that neural networks can be used to identify the best strategies, even when trained on small datasets. This is an encouraging result for the use of neural networks in offline indexing strategies. Further research is needed to fully realize the potential of neural networks in this area. A new method for determining the mixing and mass parameters of Majorana neutrinos has been proposed, utilizing a novel approach that combines astronomical data with neutrino experiments. This novel approach involves correlating the cosmic neutrino flux with parameters derived from a competition between the two sources of neutrino-antineutrino oscillations, namely, the standard source and the cosmic source. By incorporating the competition parameters along with the astronomical data into a likelihood function, the method enables the estimation of the mixing and mass parameters of Majorana neutrinos. This novel approach has been successfully tested using a simulated dataset of neutrino events from Super-Kamiokande, resulting in estimated probabilities of $0.25^{+0.05}_{-0.03}$ for $|\Delta m^{2}_{21}|$, $0.25^{+0.05}_{-0.03}$ for $\sin^{2} \theta_{12}$, $-0.5^{+0.7}_{-0.2}$ for $\delta$, $-0.5^{+0.7}_{-0.2}$ for $\delta m^{2}_{31}$, $-0.5^{+0.7}_{-0.2}$ for $\sin^{2} \theta_{31}$, and $-0.5^{+0.7}_{-0.2}$ for $m_{ee}$. The method's results are in agreement with the current best estimates of these parameters, derived from a global fit of the Standard Model. This novel approach offers a new avenue for determining the mixing and mass parameters of Majorana neutrinos, providing a supplementary method to the current experimental and theoretical frameworks. Its potential applications in future astronomical missions and neutrino experiments are being explored. To gain a deeper understanding of scholars' work habits, we analyzed a dataset of 50 academics' calendar events over the course of one month. This involved examining the frequency and duration of various types of events and exploring their interconnections. Our research revealed that professors typically hold around six in-person meetings per week, with a significant majority occurring between 9 and 10 am. In addition, we observed that in-person meetings frequently coincide with on-campus research time, while faculty members consistently update their calendar on Mondays. These findings suggest that the recorded data reflects a significant portion of faculty members' work. This research demonstrates the value of leveraging digital data to comprehend academic work patterns and presents potential research avenues for exploring this area further. Data and code used in the study are publicly available for replication and further research. We consider a region within the plane, connected and non-empty, that extends infinitely in all directions. We introduce a novel method for object handling in unstructured environments, dubbed Particle Driven Object Handling (PDOH). PDOH leverages a particle-based representation of an object to facilitate intuitive and efficient manipulation, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through both simulations and real-world experiments with a robotic arm. Key advantages of PDOH include its adaptability to objects of diverse shapes and its seamless integration with a wide range of end-effectors, including suction cups, grasping hands, and manipulators equipped with fingers or claws. Furthermore, PDOH operates without reliance on pre-existing object models, and its efficiency in handling objects of varying sizes is unaffected. A comprehensive implementation of PDOH is made available to the public. We also showcase real-world applications of PDOH, including object reorientation, placement, and sorting, and we demonstrate its potential for use in a wide range of practical settings. For example, PDOH could be utilized in warehouses to sort items, in manufacturing facilities to assemble components, and in service-based industries to perform tasks such as pouring liquids or opening packages. We believe that PDOH represents a significant step forward in the field of robotic object handling and manipulation. A video showcasing the real-world experiments can be viewed at https://youtu.be/qn4s0sJY8gA. The code implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/etherean/pdoh. We invite researchers to contribute to the development of our code through pull requests. We are also interested in collaborating with researchers to apply PDOH in real-world settings and to develop new applications. We explore two key challenges: ensuring the central node receives a representative sample of the network, and mitigating the impact of variability in the quantization process. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of MetaKernel, with notable improvements in its ability to capture the range of random characteristics and produce high-quality images with as few as 10 labeled examples. Intention forecasting aims to predict the future actions of autonomous entities by analyzing their current behavior. This task is particularly challenging when the future plans are not explicitly linked to current actions. We propose an approach to improve intention forecasting by leveraging a representation of the future plans. This representation is derived from a set of images that illustrate the planned path. Our method combines a neural network that predicts the future plans with an intention forecasting model that takes both into account. We evaluate our method on a dataset of autonomous vehicles and find that incorporating path representation yields better results, especially in scenarios with limited training data. Our method outperforms existing baselines in these scenarios, achieving significant gains in accuracy. Our findings suggest that incorporating path representation is a valuable strategy for improving intention forecasting, especially in resource-constrained environments. This approach has broader applications beyond autonomous vehicles, including any scenario where future intentions can be visually represented. We make our code available for further research.

The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly altered the research landscape across various fields, including biology, where the virus's discovery in December 2019 already started influencing research direction and focus. This study examines the pandemic's impact on the biological sciences research community from the outbreak's onset until September 2021 through a comprehensive analysis of publication trends, author collaboration, and inter-disciplinary research connections in papers from the DOAJ and PubMed databases. Our analysis reveals a substantial increase in biological sciences-related publications following the pandemic, with a notable spike in the second quarter of 2020 and sustained growth throughout the year. Our results also indicate a rise in single-author publications and increased collaboration during this period, as well as a shift towards more inter-disciplinary research. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a significant surge in publications related to the SARS-CoV-2 virus and COVID-19 across all areas of biology, with the greatest impact in the fields of microbiology, immunology, and virology. Our study also highlights the emergence of emerging fields such as computational biology, computational medicine, and computational life sciences. Overall, this research provides a detailed understanding of the pandemic's effect on the biological sciences research community. Our analysis offers a valuable framework for researchers to track the evolution of inter-disciplinary fields and changes in research focus in response to significant global events. We investigate a specific quantization procedure for quiver representations that can be viewed as a numerical approximation of a particular algebra within the quantum Schur wedge. Our main findings are two key theorems. Firstly, we demonstrate that, for quivers with no cycles, abelianization and quantization are mutually compatible. Secondly, for quivers featuring no more than two interconnected loops, abelianization and quantization are mutually commutable. These results underpin a program aimed at developing a quantized version of the Braverman-Rabinovich framework for quiver varieties. Additionally, our work includes a new proof of the Koszul dualization of the quantum Schur lemma, a novel approach to the commutativity of quantization and dehomogenization within the quantum Schur wedge, and a generalization of the Yang-Baxter equation for quiver Hamiltonians. These findings are further extended to the context of the affine Weyl group. The paper's appendices contain several supplementary results, including a proof of the quantum Schur lemma for the affine type A1 quiver and an exploration of the relationship between our work and the theory of cluster algebras. The underlying code used to generate these results is also provided. To address this challenge, we propose a new method for automatically constructing call graphs for evolving software systems. ENOS achieves this by identifying non-sensitive DNN layers and relocating them to energy-efficient storage, while ensuring rapid data transfer and minimizing data duplication. ENOS also leverages a novel hybrid architecture that combines conventional DRAM and ENMs to create a robust Neural Network Administrator (NNA) that optimizes DNN execution. The Gumbel-max algorithm has garnered significant attention in the realm of deep learning due to its ability to efficiently sample from categorical distributions. This property has led to its widespread adoption in the estimation of uncertainties such as discretized probabilistic outcomes and classification uncertainties. This paper serves as a comprehensive overview of the Gumbel-max algorithm along with various extensions addressing multi-class and multi-label problems, as well as general-purpose categorical distributions. Furthermore, we examine strategies for mitigating the high computational requirements of the Gumbel-max algorithm, often a major obstacle to its practical implementation. To this end, we evaluate the efficacy of cutting-edge approaches for large-scale deep learning applications. This paper also delves into the theoretical underpinnings of the Gumbel-max technique, providing an in-depth exploration of the relationship between the Gumbel-max algorithm and the Gibbs sampler. Finally, we discuss the potential avenues for future research in the field. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first comprehensive survey of the Gumbel-max technique and its extensions. We hope this contribution will facilitate the development of more reliable and efficient uncertainty estimation methods for deep learning models. This work is intended to be a self-contained resource for machine learning professionals, providing an accessible introduction to the Gumbel-max algorithm and its applications in the process. Additionally, this comprehensive overview is designed to serve as a valuable reference for researchers in the field, offering a thorough understanding of the Gumbel-max algorithm and its extensions. Monocular vision has significant implications for 3D object recognition, a pivotal challenge in computer vision. However, this task is complicated by the inherent ambiguity of 2D images when it comes to their corresponding 3D objects. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages the depth information extracted from stereo images to condition dynamic attention. This depth-based attention effectively prioritizes the most critical pixels in the RGB image for 3D object recognition, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our method. Our approach, dubbed Depth-conditioned Dynamic Information Transmission for Monocular 3D Object Recognition (DD-IT), consists of a multi-component framework that includes a depth-based attention module, an enhanced RGB image processing module, and a depth-aided monocular 3D object recognition module. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our proposed method, achieving a notable improvement of 2.2% over the current state-of-the-art for 3D object recognition. These structures, formed by stacking two photonic honeycomb lattices, exhibit unique characteristics that are not present in their individual components. Furthermore, we show that the flat bands are protected by the chiral symmetry of the underlying moiré Hamiltonian. Notably, we also find that the flat bands are susceptible to localization effects due to the presence of a nearly-flat dispersive band, which can give rise to a unique, self-intersecting density of states. Our research provides a new understanding of photonic moiré physics and offers a practical approach to achieving flat bands in photonic systems. Moreover, it opens up new avenues for exploring the complex interplay between localization, flat bands, and self-intersecting density of states in photonic systems. The developed concept can be applied to other photonic systems with moiré patterns and may also be relevant to other fields, such as quantum Hall physics. Ultimately, this study paves the way for the creation of new photonic devices and systems with novel properties. The widespread adoption of MPLS has significantly increased its scope, yet its inherent nature often conceals its data from external detection, limiting network monitoring tools. This research presents TNT, a system capable of uncovering an organization's entire MPLS network topology, starting from a single entry point. TNT's unique approach involves utilizing the organization's network within the organization's private MPLS network, generating traffic patterns that allow TNT to identify and understand the organization's entire network structure, including hidden L2 networks and remote networks beyond the initial entry point. We have tested TNT on a large university campus with an extensive 12,000-node MPLS network and demonstrated its ability to significantly improve network visibility. Our evaluation shows TNT to be highly efficient, requiring minimal time to generate a comprehensive map of the entire network. This map not only includes the immediate network but also reveals a substantial portion of the remote network infrastructure, including 2,000 nodes beyond the initial entry point. Our research indicates that TNT can be used to improve network security, enhance network resilience, and optimize network operations, including traffic engineering and network security. Extracting structured data from unorganized text has been a long-standing challenge for artificial intelligence.  Addressing this challenge, open information extraction systems aim to automatically identify and collect facts from online content without preconceived notions.  Current open information extraction systems, although effective, have significant limitations, primarily due to their inability to tie contextual information to the facts they extract.  This results in a lack of understanding of the specific setting in which a fact was extracted, ultimately limiting their practical utility.  To overcome these constraints, we introduce Graphene, an innovative system that utilizes a graph-based approach to connect extracted facts with their corresponding contexts.  This graph structure enables Graphene to effectively capture the full context of the fact, including the specific words surrounding it and the sentences in which they are expressed.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted a thorough evaluation of Graphene's performance on three public open information extraction benchmarks, resulting in superior performance compared to existing systems, with the added benefit of context preservation.  To facilitate further research, the Graphene system and accompanying data will be made publicly available.  A video demonstration of this method can be found at https://youtu.be/6s8s5qzKQ8A. This framework is grounded in the Navier-Stokes equations and incorporates a novel loss function based on the absolute flux differences between simulated and predicted flow fields. Our method demonstrates high accuracy in permeability estimation, particularly for porous media with moderate to high permeability, according to comparisons with historical data. However, for rocks with low permeability, the predicted results are overestimated, suggesting that the physical constraints of the physics-informed network are overly influenced by the low-permeability rocks' smooth flow field. Clothing cones are a universal, three-dimensional framework for understanding and representing the diverse, dynamic properties of various types of garments. By encapsulating key properties of clothing, such as stretchiness, thinness, and the way they move when stretched, these cones offer a way to standardize and simplify the process of computer-aided fashion design. Through a series of experiments and visual comparisons, we confirm the superiority of this approach over existing methods for representing the behavior of clothing, and demonstrate its versatility and potential for application across a range of challenging tasks. Bilevel optimization problems, commonly encountered in engineering and economic contexts, pose significant challenges due to their complex dynamics. Specifically, these problems exhibit characteristics such as mixed-ordered derivatives and high complexity, which hinder their assessment using traditional tools. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel method, known as second-order reactivity examination, which leverages functional derivatives to evaluate the performance of these complex problems. By applying this approach, we have gained valuable insights into the behavior of these problems, and have demonstrated its effectiveness through the analysis of various numerical examples. Furthermore, our results reveal that second-order reactivity examination offers a more comprehensive analysis compared to other methods, such as the second-order condition examination. Additionally, our findings suggest that second-order reactivity examination has the potential to be applied to problems involving non-differentiable constraints. To this end, we have explored the feasibility of extending our method to these types of problems, and have identified a potential approach for doing so. The results presented in this paper are likely to contribute significantly to the ongoing research efforts in the field of complex optimization problems. A recent paper presented a pair of nonlinear equations for describing small amplitude surface waves on water, a topic that is receiving increasing attention due to its connection to the COVID-19 pandemic. Human activity analysis in natural settings has been a long-standing focus of computer vision research, with the development of activity recognition systems to support a range of applications. However, existing datasets are often limited in their coverage of human activity and setting, which restricts the scope of activity recognition tasks. We introduce ViT-BEVSeg, a transformer-based deep learning architecture for monocular aerial segmentation, which utilizes a novel bird's eye view representation to process global context efficiently. By converting aerial images into a top-down perspective, ViT-BEVSeg enhances the network's performance significantly. We evaluate ViT-BEVSeg on the Semantic Segmentation in Natural Scenes dataset and achieve competitive results with a mean IoU score of 68.94%. The accompanying code and pre-trained model will be released publicly. ViT-BEVSeg demonstrates substantial improvements over traditional convolution-based methods, which are trained solely on a single dataset. Extensive experiments conducted on various aerial datasets reveal that ViT-BEVSeg outperforms existing methods, showcasing its effectiveness in real-world applications. The task of open-set identification involves determining whether an input belongs to a recognized class or not. Unlike standard classification where inputs from unknown classes will be assigned to a specific 'unknown' class, this problem requires identifying inputs from both known and unknown classes. Current methods often utilize a binary classifier to differentiate between known classes and a single unknown class. However, these methods have a limitation in that they do not account for the possibility of multiple unknown classes. In this study, a new approach is proposed that utilizes a triplet loss to learn feature representations that distinguish inputs from multiple unknown classes. The proposed method incorporates an augmentation-driven similarity loss to learn feature representations that maintain similarity within known classes while distinguishing them from unknown classes. The proposed method has been tested on various image and text datasets and has achieved state-of-the-art performance. The source code is available for public access. To facilitate further research, a new benchmark for open-set identification has been established, including a new dataset and evaluation metrics, which can be found at https://github.com/keonlee123/OSI. We've developed a unique laser model featuring an excitatory microcavity with delayed optical feedback, which enables the creation of complex pulse patterns through a single resonant frequency. By adjusting a single control parameter, we can seamlessly transition between various stable pulse states, including fixed-frequency and frequency-increments regimes, as well as stable continuous-wave operation. Interestingly, we've observed that these pulse patterns can be separated into distinct frequency ranges, a phenomenon that occurs when the delay is sufficiently long. Our study also reveals that these stable states are remarkably insensitive to changes in the feedback delay, a finding that bodes well for experimental implementation. Specifically, we've demonstrated that these pulse patterns can be achieved with delays as short as 100 picoseconds, a timeframe that falls within the capabilities of current experimental technology. Furthermore, we've shown that these stable states can be maintained through a combination of pump intensity fluctuations and intrinsic noise, phenomena that can be readily observed using experimental techniques. Overall, our research has revealed a wealth of stable states in microcavities with delayed optical feedback, many of which have yet to be experimentally confirmed. The insights gained from this study will serve as a valuable guide for researchers seeking to explore the rich dynamical behavior of microcavities with delayed optical feedback. The techniques and findings presented in this work can be readily adapted to study a broader range of systems, including lasers with coherent excitation, delayed optoelectric feedback, and other systems exhibiting excitatory nonlinearity. The study of these systems will continue to yield new insights into the fundamental physics of lasers and will pave the way for the development of advanced photonic technologies. The code and data supporting this research have been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/tpwalther/Excitable_Microcavity. Additional resources, including movies of the stable states and associated time series, can be found on this website at https://sites.google.com/view.tpwalther/home. Finally, we encourage readers to explore the rich dynamics of our system model by adjusting the parameters using an interactive interface available at the same aforementioned website.
